titleStmt.title: Traffic Scheduling Coprocessor with Schedulability Analysis Capability

analytic.title: Traffic Scheduling Coprocessor with Schedulability Analysis Capability

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The low processing power of typical fieldbus nodes used in real-time applications usually limits the sort of message scheduling that can be done, and precludes any kind of on-line schedulability analysis. Moving these computationally intensive tasks to dedicated hardware is an effective way to remove this limitation and achieve the best temporal determinism.

This paper presents a traffic scheduling and schedulability analyser coprocessor targeted for centralised scheduling fieldbus systems. The FPGA-based coprocessor generates message schedules according to one of three drferent scheduling policies, and allows the number of messages and their respective parameters to be changed dynamically. The schedulability analyser capability supports on-line admission control of new messages. The paper starts by discussing the basic features which such a coprocessor should include. Then the coprocessor architecture is described together with several relevant implementation details. Finally the worst case execution times of its two main functions are derived, validating the coprocessor's feasibility.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Message scheduling on a fieldbus can be done statically or dynamically. Table driven and priority-based approaches such as the ones used in WorldFIP and CAN respectively, fall in the category of static scheduling, while the best-effort approach adopted for Profibus is typical of the dynamic category [I].

In what concerns real-time applications such as process control, we are interested in scheduling messages in a way that guarantees their timeliness constraints. Here, the static scheduling approach seems to be the right choice. However if the application requirements also call for a certain operational flexibility in what concerns connecting or removing equipment from the fieldbus, or changing its configuration on-line, then the static approach is no longer adequate. In this respect, that is, in terms of operational flexibility, the dynamic scheduler would be the natural choice. However, besides its inability to guarantee timely operation by itself, the dynamic scheduler also imposes a higher run-time overhead. The run-time overhead is usually a sensitive issue due to the limited processing power generally available in fieldbus nodes. Since we are considering centralised scheduling this concerns in particular the node where the scheduler executes, known as the arbiter node. One effective solution to off-load the CPU in the arbiter node is to transfer the scheduling task to dedicated hardware working as a slave coprocessor (see figure 1). Ideally such a coprocessor should be capable of accepting dynamic changes in the message set, and run a schedulability analysis in order to guarantee that all deadlines are met.

Specialised coprocessors have been used for long in implementing critical functions of hard real-time operating systems. Two basic approaches have been explored in their implementation: microprocessor-based solutions, and custom VLSI designs.

The former concept was adopted in a number of research projects such as the ones reported in [2] and [ 3 ] , and provides all the flexibility of software-based solutions. The custom design approach, be it based on ASIC technology or programmable logic devices, provides arguably the fastest and most deterministic execution times, and is the basis of many coprocessors described in the literature.

The ASIC RTU [4] implements all the basic functionality of a multitasking multiprocessing real-time operating system kernel, while the SSCoP [5] is a specialised task scheduling coprocessor with schedulability evaluation capability. Another example is the task scheduling coprocessor reported in [6] which has, conceptually, some similarities with the coprocessor described here.

For traffic scheduling in fieldbus systems little work has been done in the development of dedicated hardware. The Planning Scheduler CoProcessor (PSCoP) [7,8] developed by our team, was the first FPGA-based solution to appear addressing the specific requirements of traffic scheduling in CAN, particularly in the framework of the FTT-CAN (Flexible Time-Triggered on CAN) protocol [

In this paper a new message scheduling coprocessor is presented. It builds on the lessons learned with PSCoP and it is now a completely dynamic scheduler with a whole new functionality, including a schedulability analyser.

The next section starts with a presentation of the coprocessor features, and explains the reasons which led us to include some of them. The coprocessor is then fully described, first by presenting its interface to the node CPU in Section 3, and then by discussing its internal structure and behaviour at the register-transfer level, in Section 4. Finally, in Section 5, we characterise the coprocessor performance by deriving its worst case execution times.

div.head: Basic Features of the Coprocessor
div.p: With the development of PSCoP a great deal of insight was gained on the levels of performance that can be attained with FPGA technology. Being implemented on a XC401OXL FPGA and running at a mere 12 MHz, PSCoP exhibited a remarkable performance by being able to generate message-schedules for a fixed time interval (a plan), in less than 1% of the time needed to dispatch that same interval [7]. This suggested that we could sacrifice some of the performance room in favour of a few design improvements and additional functionality.
PSCoP based its operation on the planning scheduler

[ l ]an hybrid scheduling method with a part of the timeliness characteristics of static scheduling, and a fraction of the flexibility of dynamic scheduling. So, in defining the successor of PSCoP, one of the first decisions was to improve on the operational flexibility aspect, which resulted in the adoption of a fully dynamic scheduler model. The coprocessor schedules message transactions in fixed duration time slots, called the Elementary Cycles (ECs). The bus time is assumed as being divided in ECs, which represent the basic time unit in which message periods are expressed. The coprocessor builds one ECschedule at a time.

Having a single EC-schedule output, guarantees that all changes in the message set are accounted for in the next EC-schedule, thus ensuring the highest responsiveness. (In process control applications this can range from 1 to IOms, which is the typical EC duration).

However, preventing the coprocessor to build several ECschedules in advance as PSCoP is able to, doesn't allow it to anticipate the missing of deadlines as in the planning scheduler. To solve this problem we introduced a schedulability analysis capability in the coprocessor. Therefore, every time the message set is changed, we can run the analysis to check if the set is still schedulable. Scheduling is resumed only if the analysis indicated a schedulable set.

In PSCoP, scheduling is ruled by a static priority-based policy. Pursuing a goal of maximum flexibility, the new coprocessor was defined supporting a few other useful scheduling policies between which operation can be changed dynamically.

div.head: Coprocessor Interface
div.p: Table I -Scheduling policy control bits.
The coprocessor has a standard peripheral-like interface for connection to the node CPU. This interface provides access to the set of registers depicted in figure 2.

Variable's Parameters Register Slots -These registers hold the parameters of each message to be scheduled. There are 32 slots of registers for a maximum of 32 messages. Each slot contains five 8-bit registers, where the parameters of each message should be written to prior to any scheduling or schedulability analysis operation.

The message's priority, optionally written to the priority register (PriReg), has a range of 0 (highest priority) to 255. The values written to the phase (PhaReg), period (PerReg) and deadline (DeaReg) registers are expressed in number of ECs. A register slot has no message allocated to it if its period register is cleared. The values written to the message duration register (DurReg) should be expressed in a normalised unit given by NECd = (EC Duration / 255). If a message has a duration of At time units, its corresponding DurReg register should have the value rAt / NECdl . The deadline value written in the DeaReg register is only relevant for schedulability analysis.

Bit number i corresponds to the message assigned to register slot i. Go/Done -The node CPU sets this bit to command the coprocessor to generate an EC-schedule (if SA=O) or perform a schedulability analysis (if SA=l). The coprocessor resets this bit when done. NS -After the coprocessor is instructed to do a schedulability analysis, NS becoming 1 means that the set is not schedulable.

div.head: Coprocessor Architecture
div.p: The scheduling task comprises two basic activities: the action of placement of transactions in the ECs, and the function of keeping track of the instants in time when each message must be produced. In the coprocessor these activities are carried out by the EC-Schedule Builder (ECSB) and the Variable's Production Timer (VPT), respectively. A similar partitioning approach can be found in the task scheduling coprocessor described in [6].

Figure 3 depicts the coprocessor architecture with one ECSB and 32 VPTs connected through an internal bus. Each message to be scheduled is allocated to one VPT unit which holds the message's period (P), initial phase (Ph), deadline (D) and priority (Pr) parameters. VPTs are thus the physical image of the message's parameters register slots of the coprocessor programmer's model.

Global timing information received from the ECSB allows all VPTs to be synchronised while keeping track of the EC-schedule currently being generated. When a VPT detects that the scheduling for a particular EC where its message should be produced has started, it signals the To check the schedulability of a message set the coprocessor executes a response time-based schedulability analysis using the timeline method [l], as detailed below.

div.head: The Variable's Production Timer
div.p: The internal structure of each VPT unit is represented in figure 4. The registers PriReg, PerReg and DeaReg of the coprocessor programmer's model (figure 2) are physically implemented in a register file inside the VPT.

There are two presetable decrement counters, the Allocation Counter (AC) and the Deadline Counter (DC). AC is used to keep track of the message's release time. DC is used in the schedulability analysis to evaluate if the

There is no dedicated register for the phase parameter. What is mapped in the PhaReg position of the register slot is the AC counter, which is thus initially set with the phase value.

The AC counter is decremented by one every time the ECSB starts a new EC-schedule. When AC reaches zero, indicating the message should be produced, the Allocation Control Unit (AIICU) requests the message allocation to ECSB.

Because more than one VPT can request allocation in the same EC, a mechanism exists to decide which request to serve first. This selection mechanism is based on a serial self-selection arbiter distributed by all the VPTs. Contention is resolved using dynamic priority vectors which are derived from message parameters such as their period or priority, making it easy to implement wellknown scheduling policies, and to switch dynamically between them as desired.

The arbiter is implemented by the Arbitration Shift Register (ArbSReg) and the Arbitration Control Unit (ArbCU) in each VPT. The priority vectors have 13 bits as shown in figure 5. The most significant 8 bits are taken from the priority, period or deadline register, as dictated by the SP[l,O] bits of CSReg. The least significant 5 bits are equal to the VPT identifier, which is hardwired in the IDReg register.

div.head: VPT Operating Modes
div.p: The VPT and the ECSB have two operating modes: the Scheduler Mode (or S-Mode) and the Analyser Mode (or A-Mode), which correspond, respectively, to the coprocessor functions of scheduler and schedulability analyser.

In the middle of its normal scheduler operation, the coprocessor may be asked to do a schedulability analysis, and then to resume scheduling from the point where it was interrupted. T o do this the VPTs must save their state in S-Mode before switching to A-Mode. The state information to save, which will be needed on return from A-Mode, is the current value in AC and a bit indicating whether or not the VPT has a pending request. The

div.head: Scheduler mode (S-Mode); b)-Flowchart in Schedulability Analysis mode (A-Mode).
div.p: resources holding this information during a schedulability analysis are, respectively, the Allocation Counter Register (ACR) and the State Flag Register (S) in figure 4. Figure 6 depicts the operation flowcharts of the VPT in its two modes. The transitions between modes are detailed in figure 7.

S-Mode -In the S-Mode (figure 6-a), after all registers have been initialised, the VPTs sit idle in state S ~S , waiting for ECSB to start building the first EC-schedule. When the GolDone bit is set in the CSReg, ECSB initiates a series of cycles in which it receives the IDS of VPTs requesting the allocation of their messages in the current EC. With a collection of these IDS, ECSB builds the EC-schedule.

The VPT uses its AC counter as shown, with the phase and period parameters, to keep track of the EC where its message should be allocated. When the processing for that particular EC-schedule begins, the VPT raises a request. Next an arbitration cycle decides which among the VPTs requesting allocation, can send its ID to ECSB. For a message to be successfully allocated, its VPT must not only win the arbitration, but also it must receive a positive acknowledge from ECSB indicating that the message's transaction fits in the EC.

Many arbitration cycles may be generated as part of each EC-schedule processing. If a VPT was not able to allocate its message in the first arbitration cycle, it waits for the next while keeping its request active. Eventually the current EC may be closed before the VFT is able to allocate successfully. In this case the VPT continues asserting its request while waiting for the next EC, where the message allocation is tried once more.

Between the processing of EC-schedules, VPTs are idle in either states Sls or SZs. In this condition the message set may be changed by the CPU (the coprocessor idle state is indicated by a zero in bit GolDone in CSReg).
All parameters of existing messages can be changed. In particular, changes in the message's period are guaranteed to be made without any spurious transient.
A-Mode -As can be seen from figure 6-b, the VPT flowchart in A-Mode is very similar to the S-Mode flowchart. The difference is basically the utilisation of the Deadline Counter (DC).

In testing the schedulability of the message set, what the coprocessor does is to check that the response time experienced by each message is always below its respective deadline value. Theory shows that, if we assume a null initial phase, it is enough to do this response time analysis at time zero only [I]. In other words, if we guarantee that the first allocation of each message is made within its deadline, then we can assure the schedulability of the set.

To check individual response times we build what is known as the timeline. This consists basically in constructing the EC-schedules in the normal way, until all messages are allocated at least once. If we succeed in doing this without any missed deadline, then the set is guaranteed to be schedulable.

To implement this method, the coprocessor needs little more than the scheduling functionality. In particular the VPT needs just to use the DC counter to monitor the delay between the message's release and its allocation. If this delay exceeds the message's deadline, ECSB is signalled.

div.head: EC-Schedule Builder
div.p: This module builds EC-schedules in scheduler mode, and controls the coprocessor operation in analyser mode. Figure 8 shows the ECSB architecture together with the node CPU interface unit.

As we saw above, the ECSB builds EC-schedules by accepting requests for allocation from the VPTs. The start of processing of a new EC-schedule (in scheduler or analyser mode) is communicated to all VPTs by a global signal, which the VPTs use to decrement their internal counters, and to know therefore when they should request the release of their respective messages.

If there are requests, ECSB triggers a first arbitration cycle, at the end of which it acquires the ID of the highest priority VPT. The ID is captured in the register AddLatch, and used as an index to the table MDLut. This is a RAM look-up table where the DurReg registers are physically mapped. The transaction duration of the corresponding message is thus retrieved from this table to check if the transaction fits in the EC, or its remaining free time (if we are already past the first allocation). To check this, ECSB keeps track of the total EC time already booked by previous transactions in the Acc Register. The new transaction time is thus accumulated to the value in this register. Due to the normalisation of transaction times, if the time just added exceeds the time left in the EC. this addition results in an overflow condition. In case there is no overflow, the message is allocated in the EC. This allocation is recorded in ECSReg by the Decoder module using the ID in the AddLatch, which sets the bit located in the bit position corresponding to the VPT just served. A signal sent at the end of the arbitration cycle, tells the VPT that the allocation was made, allowing it to withdraw its allocation request. In case there are more pending requests from other VPTs, the ECSB initiates another arbitration cycle. This sequence is repeated until all requests are served, or ECSB finds an allocation request whose transaction exceeds the remaining time in the EC. In the latter case the message is not allocated, and the EC-schedule is closed. No more arbitration cycles are generated, which means that pending requests are deferred until the next EC-schedule is processed. In scheduler mode the GolDone bit is reset and the coprocessor goes idle.

In analyser mode the ECSB works basically the same way, with the exception that it does not stop after completing an EC-schedule. In this mode the ECSB simulates the construction of successive EC-schedules. It stops doing this only if a VFT detects the missing of a deadline, or if all VPTs succeed in allocating their messages at least once. Each of these conditions is communicated by a dedicated bus line to ECSB, which terminates the analysis by updating the NS flag in CSReg according to the result.
Note that, contrary to the VPT modules, the ECSB does not require the saving of any state information before switching to analyser mode.

div.head: Preliminary Feasibility Assessment
div.p: The performance requirements that the coprocessor must fulfil are basically two: First it must be able to generate an EC-schedule within the time it takes to dispatch the previous one. Secondly, it must be fast enough to run a schedulability analysis within the same EC dispatching time. Clearly these two requirements are related, and in particular the fulfilment of the latter implies that the first one is also satisfied.

At the time of writing the coprocessor is still in the early stages of development, so, for now, no simulation or real performance figures are available to assess the coprocessor's feasibility within the requirements stated above. Nevertheless, an estimate of performance was obtained, by carrying out a step by step analysis of the various phases of the coprocessor's internal operation, counting the number of clock cycles required by each.

Taking into account some associated control activity, we counted a total of 16 clock cycles per message allocation. If we add another 3 clock cycles that the ECSB requires for synchronisation and control, we can express the coprocessor scheduling time (in clock cycles) by t,, = 3 + 16. For a set of nine messages this microcontroller takes 7.8ms to output a single EC-schedule. If we had, let say, a 200MHz CPU in the scheduler node, which corresponds to a speed-up factor of 18 (ignoring, for simplicity sake, performance gains due to architectural enhancements) we could expect a similar reduction in the scheduling time, to about 4 3 0 ~s . Assuming an EC duration of Ims we would be left now with 57% of the EC time for schedulability tests. Clearly this is much less than what we can achieve with the 20MHz FPGA-based coprocessor. Increasing even further the microprocessor clock will shorten the scheduling time, but will also raise costs and power dissipation problems, which are both sensitive issues in CAN systems.

For any given scenario we can also calculate the value of k,, for which there is time to do a schedulability analysis. If we assume a rate-monotonic scheduling policy, this means that the coprocessor is able to evaluate within Ims, the schedulability of a set containing messages with periods as high as 47ms.

div.head: Concluding Remarks
div.p: In this paper we described a coprocessor capable of traffic scheduling and schedulability analysis in a fieldbus-based distributed system. The coprocessor is particularly adapted to the FIT-CAN protocol but can be explored also in other centralised scheduling fieldbuses.

The coprocessor has a simple and powerful CPU interface, supports three distinct scheduling policies (ratemonotonic, deadline-monotonic and priority-based), and is completely dynamic, meaning that all message parameters can be changed on-line in between scheduling operations. A first prototype implemented on a XC4000family FPGA with support for up to 32 messages, is under development.

The performance analysis revealed excellent results concerning the worst case scheduling time. As for the time the coprocessor takes to do a schedulability analysis, although the results are not so spectacular, they are still very promising despite the highly pessimistic assumptions used.
Further validation is now being carried out using more realistic message loads, provided by the PSA (Peugeot SocietC Automobile) and S A E (Society of Automotive Engineering) benchmarks.
